Nigeria’s push to cut costly petrol dependence and harness its natural gas reserves is gaining momentum as the Federal Government deploys MDGIF to accelerate CNG adoption, DARE OLAWIN reports The removal of petrol subsidy has increased the urgency of the government’s gas development agenda, particularly as rising fuel prices continue to put pressure on transport operators, businesses and households. Although Nigeria has abundant natural gas reserves, inadequate infrastructure for transporting, processing and distributing the commodity has continued to limit its domestic utilisation. As far as the government is concerned, the challenge is no longer simply to make gas available but to develop the facilities required to move it from production points to industries, businesses, power plants and vehicles. In the transportation sector, the shortage of CNG refuelling stations has remained a major obstacle to the transition from petrol-powered vehicles, despite the potential savings associated with the alternative fuel. The long queues in the few CNG refuelling stations testify to the rise in CNG adoption despite the infrastructure gap. This infrastructure deficit has brought the MDGIF into sharper focus as the government seeks to use the fund to stimulate investments across the gas value chain. Established under the Petroleum Industry Act, the fund is designed to support projects that improve the transportation and processing of natural gas, as well as its distribution and utilisation. Managed by the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority, the MDGIF is expected to attract more than $575bn in investments into Nigeria’s gas sector, expand midstream and downstream infrastructure and create a more robust domestic gas market. Its growing intervention in the CNG segment was recently demonstrated in Lagos, where five daughter and last-mile retail stations developed by the Ibile Oil and Gas Corporation with support from the fund were unveiled. The facilities, situated in Idimu and Abule Egba in Alimosho, Ogolonto in Ikorodu West, Ajah in Eti-Osa and Oko-Oba in Agege, are expected to bring natural gas closer to motorists and commercial transport operators in different parts of Lagos. The fund has also completed CNG stations in some federal universities to ease transport burdens among students. The unveiling represents another phase of the Federal Government’s efforts to expand the country’s CNG network and encourage more Nigerians to switch from petrol to gas. Speaking at the event, the Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas) and Chairman of the MDGIF Governing Council, Ekperikpe Ekpo, said the projects aligned with President Bola Tinubu’s directive to accelerate the development of CNG infrastructure nationwide. He recalled that the President had directed the establishment of an additional 500 refuelling stations as part of a broader plan to build a national network of 1,000 facilities. “Through the Renewed Hope Agenda, the President has made it clear that Nigeria’s abundant gas resources must work for Nigerians. They must power our industries, support businesses, improve transportation, create employment and, ultimately, reduce the cost pressures faced by ordinary citizens,” Ekpo said. Each of the five stations has a compression capacity of 24,000 standard cubic metres of gas per day and storage capacity of 9,800 standard cubic metres. Collectively, the facilities have a reported storage capacity of approximately 45,640 standard cubic metres and can fill about 8,400 vehicles daily at full capacity. The stations will utilise locally produced natural gas, supporting the government’s efforts to increase domestic consumption and reduce dependence on petrol and diesel in the transportation sector. For the Executive Director of the MDGIF, Oluwole Adama, the projects demonstrate how investments in gas infrastructure can translate into economic benefits for ordinary Nigerians. “Under the Renewed Hope Agenda, our gas reserves are being put to work to power transport, commerce, jobs and the everyday needs of Nigerians. The Fund exists to expand viable gas infrastructure and ensure that Nigeria’s gas resources are used productively, and the projects we commission today show what that looks like on the ground,” the MDGIF boss stated. Adama maintained that the benefits of the stations would extend beyond the physical facilities to commercial drivers, traders, fleet operators and commuters who depend on road transportation. He cited the danfo driver in Abule Egba, the tricycle operator navigating Ikorodu Road, the trader transporting goods to Mile 12 market and the young professional commuting from Ajah as potential beneficiaries of improved access to CNG. Fleet owners could also benefit from lower and more predictable energy costs, while businesses involved in the movement of goods could reduce their transportation expenses. However, the extent to which these potential savings will reach commuters depends on the level of adoption, consistent gas supply and the willingness of transport operators to pass on lower operating costs through reduced fares. Many Nigerians have observed that motorists who benefitted from the Federal Government’s free CNG conversion programmes still charge the same fares as those using premium motor spirit. Gas infrastructure shortfall The MDGIF’s importance to Nigeria’s gas development ambitions lies in its broader mandate beyond the provision of CNG refuelling stations. The fund is designed to stimulate investments in infrastructure across the midstream and downstream segments of the petroleum industry. Midstream activities involve the transportation, storage and processing of natural gas, while downstream infrastructure supports its distribution and utilisation by end users. The distinction is important because the development of a viable domestic gas market requires an interconnected network of pipelines, processing plants, storage facilities, distribution systems and consumption infrastructure. Without adequate midstream facilities, gas producers may struggle to transport their output to markets. Similarly, the absence of downstream infrastructure can prevent available gas from reaching industries, businesses, households and motorists. The MDGIF is therefore expected to address some of these constraints by supporting viable projects and attracting investments into areas where infrastructure shortages have restricted the growth of the domestic market. Its target of attracting more than $575bn in investments underscores the scale of capital required to develop the country’s gas resources and expand their economic applications. Attracting private capital into the sector is particularly important to the nation because the scale of infrastructure development required cannot be sustained through public funding alone. The MDGIF is expected to provide catalytic support for projects, encourage investors and create opportunities for partnerships between government agencies, state governments and private sector operators. Its intervention in the CNG market is one example of how the fund is being deployed to stimulate infrastructure development and increase domestic gas consumption. In two years, the fund has supported the delivery and commissioning of more than 25 fully operational CNG stations nationwide, according to Adama. Its portfolio currently comprises 31 projects involving 205 infrastructure assets across the country. The figures indicate an expanding intervention in a sector where the availability of infrastructure will largely determine the pace of adoption. However, the bigger test will be whether the projects can remain commercially viable, attract sufficient patronage and deliver the expected economic benefits. ‘Govs must take responsibility for power crisis’ Tinubu’s achievements under-reported – RMRDC DG Oil industry looking up Lagos expands network The five newly commissioned facilities form part of a wider CNG development programme being implemented by the Lagos State Government through the Ibile Oil and Gas Corporation. The corporation has a mandate to deliver 15 CNG stations across the state. Four were commissioned earlier, while the five recently unveiled bring the number delivered to nine. The remaining six are expected to be completed by the first quarter of 2027. The expansion is significant for Lagos, where a large proportion of residents depend on commercial buses, tricycles and other road transport services for their daily movement. The increase in petrol prices following subsidy removal has placed considerable pressure on transport operators, many of whom have adjusted fares to accommodate rising fuel expenditure. For these operators, switching to CNG could provide an opportunity to reduce operating costs, particularly if refuelling facilities are located close to their routes and gas remains consistently available. The MDGIF-backed stations are designed as daughter and last-mile retail facilities, an arrangement intended to bring gas closer to consumers rather than concentrate refuelling infrastructure around major industrial locations. This approach could improve accessibility for motorists who may otherwise have to travel long distances to obtain CNG. Adama said the projects were deliberately designed with ordinary Nigerians in mind, including drivers, traders and workers whose livelihoods depend on affordable transportation. He urged transport operators, fleet owners, businesses and public institutions to take advantage of the facilities, while calling on IOGC to maintain high standards of safety, service delivery and operational discipline. The minister also commended the Lagos State Government and IOGC for their participation, describing the collaboration as “exactly the type of Federal-State-private-sector collaboration that we must replicate across the country.” The partnership model allows the Federal Government to provide funding support through the MDGIF, while state governments and their agencies offer local implementation platforms and operational capacity. Private sector participation and regulatory oversight are also expected to support the commercial sustainability and safe operation of the facilities. Adama, however, cautioned that the commissioning of the stations should not be mistaken for the completion of the task, saying, “The real achievement will be safe operations, reliable supply, professional maintenance and lasting public confidence. At MDGIF, we want infrastructure that works every day, not infrastructure that looks impressive only on commissioning day.” CNG on campuses Beyond commercial transportation, the MDGIF has extended its intervention to tertiary institutions through campus-based CNG stations designed to reduce mobility costs for students and university workers. The initiative is part of the government’s strategy to introduce gas-powered transportation into institutions and encourage wider acceptance of alternative fuels. The first phase is expected to cover 20 tertiary institutions, with the government indicating that the programme will extend beyond the initial target. The campus facilities complement the expansion of refuelling stations in major cities and other locations where commercial transport activities are concentrated. Recently, the Federal Government opened CNG stations in four universities as part of efforts to reduce transportation costs for students and staff in tertiary institutions across the country. The facilities, located at the University of Lagos, University of Ibadan, Federal University of Technology, Akure, and Federal University Oye-Ekiti, were unveiled under the Special Palliative Relief on University Transportation, known as Project SPROUT. The Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, said the initiative was designed to address the high cost of transportation among students, particularly those who make several trips daily between their accommodation, lecture halls and laboratories. Alausa said the Federal Government planned to extend the programme to 20 federal universities, beginning with a pilot phase involving one institution from each of the six geopolitical zones. According to Adama, the inauguration of the four facilities brought the number of universities with CNG stations under the initiative to 11. Adama noted that while the fund had supported 25 fully operational CNG stations nationwide in two years, its portfolio comprised 31 projects and 205 infrastructure assets across the country. He said the facilities were part of efforts to make natural gas infrastructure accessible to Nigerians while providing opportunities for technical training and enterprise. The MDGIF Executive Director disclosed that nine other stations, mostly in northern Nigeria, would be commissioned within a few weeks. At the national level, the Federal Government is pursuing an ambitious expansion of the CNG network, with MDGIF-backed stations already commissioned in several states and more projects reportedly at advanced stages, particularly in northern Nigeria. Tinubu’s directive for an additional 500 refuelling stations towards a national target of 1,000 is expected to accelerate the rollout. The scale of the target reflects the infrastructure requirements for making CNG a viable alternative for a significant proportion of Nigeria’s vehicle fleet. However, increasing the number of stations alone may not guarantee widespread adoption. The government must also address the cost of vehicle conversion, gas availability, distribution challenges and safety concerns. Many motorists said they could not afford about N1m to convert their vehicles. Nonetheless, the attraction of CNG lies largely in its potential to reduce fuel expenditure for motorists and businesses. Industry operators have frequently cited potential savings of up to 70 per cent for vehicles running on CNG compared with petrol. For commercial drivers, lower fuel costs could improve daily earnings, while fleet operators could reduce the amount spent on energy across their businesses. The benefits could also extend to the wider economy through lower costs of transporting agricultural produce, manufactured goods and other commodities. However, the actual savings will depend on prevailing gas prices, vehicle efficiency, conversion costs and the distance motorists travel to access refuelling facilities. For many commercial drivers, the initial cost of converting petrol-powered vehicles to CNG remains a major consideration. Although the long-term savings could justify the investment, operators with limited financial capacity may find it difficult to meet the upfront expenses. The availability of certified conversion centres, trained technicians and affordable financing will, therefore, be important to the success of the programme. Safety is another critical issue. The expansion of CNG infrastructure must be accompanied by strict compliance with technical standards, proper installation of storage systems, regular inspection and effective maintenance. The government will also need to ensure that gas supply keeps pace with the expansion of refuelling facilities. A situation where motorists convert their vehicles but struggle to obtain gas could undermine public confidence in the programme. These challenges make the operational performance of the MDGIF-backed stations as important as their construction. Ekpo said the government would measure the success of the investments by their impact on businesses, transport operators and households rather than the number of projects completed. “Our objective is therefore not simply to count the number of stations commissioned. Success must ultimately be measured by impact: whether the infrastructure helps reduce operating costs for transporters and businesses, whether those savings reach commuters, and whether Nigerian families begin to feel tangible relief,” he stated. Dare Olawin Dare Olawin is a journalist at Punch Newspapers with over a decade of reporting experience. He began his career as a community reporter and now covers the energy sector, including oil, gas, electricity, and renewables. Dare’s work reflects hands-on newsroom experience, professional development through workshops and conferences, and a strong commitment to accurate and insightful journalism.
